job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Felix Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Everyone I talk to is made up for this study, so there are no right answers. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm out of the door at six-forty to catch the train to Aarhus Harbour. I work for a company that designs and installs electrical systems for big buildings, and I'm the junior on the design side. I draw wiring layouts, calculate cable sizes, and every other week they send me out with the installers to check that what I drew fits in the wall. Evenings I'm home by six, and on Wednesdays I sing in the church choir with my girlfriend Sofie.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get to this job, and what did you study?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Electrical engineering at Aarhus University, with a good result. I did a short internship at a wind turbine service firm, mostly carrying a toolbag and reading drawings. My parents have a small dairy farm outside Silkeborg, and I grew up fixing the milking machine with my father. I rent a small flat with a friend from home. I owe about eleven thousand, I have two months of costs saved, and my parents would never let me go hungry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good. Most of these big promises don't come true, and every generation has its own miracle machine. At work I'd say the tools are fine for a draft, but I'd rather check a cable size with a calculator than trust a chatbot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm content. If AI is mostly hype, then my job stays the same: draw it, build it, check it. I'd work, save, and in a few years marry Sofie. The only thing that worries me is whether pay keeps up with the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job properly, and in a year or so take the extra exam to become a certified installer, since that comes with a pay rise. I'd keep saving around two thousand kroner a month. And I'd help my father with the farm accounts on weekends, since he's behind on the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal. I've heard that big claims fade and good work doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you trust the old way over the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the old way has a name on it. If my cable is too thin and a building burns, someone points at me. I'd rather know the answer is mine. My father says you check the fence yourself, even when your neighbour built it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything in that picture bothering you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cost of living. Rent for a one-bedroom flat in Aarhus is high, and I'd like to buy something with Sofie. It's a slow plan, and I'd rather work towards it than complain.

say: Most big promises don't come true, and every generation has a **miracle machine**.
The tools are fine for a draft, but I'd rather check with a **calculator**.
think: If AI is hype, my job stays the same: **draw it**, build it, check it.
My only worry is whether **pay** keeps up with rent.
do: Take the extra exam to become a **certified installer**.
Save around **two thousand kroner** a month.
Help my father with the **farm accounts** on weekends.
feel: **Calm and normal**, because good work outlasts big claims.
S0.quote: My father says you check the fence yourself, even when your neighbour built it.
fieldNote: Trusts **accountability**: a name on the cable size.
Voice is dry, short, and rooted in **farm** sayings.
Plans work, savings and **marriage** in order, with no mention of AI hopes or fears.

steps.text: Take the certified installer exam within a year
Keep drawing and checking wiring layouts myself

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see who does the work properly. If software drafts layouts and checks numbers, fine, but someone has to answer for the building. At the pub I'd say these companies are racing, and I'd still rather see people trained than handed money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm a bit exposed, because drawing layouts and calculating cable sizes is the thinking part of electrical work. The firm might need fewer drafters and more installers and inspectors. I've no wish to use the software, and I know my boss would like me to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend more time on site with the installers, because that's the part a computer can't do, and I'd go for the installer certificate sooner. If my firm asked me to use the layout software, I'd learn it slowly and use it as a second opinion. I'd also keep my savings, and I'd ask my father if there's any work on the farm for a month if things go badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. Not for a day, but it's there in the background, like weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really learn the software you say you don't like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the job needs it, yes. I wouldn't be happy, but I'd do it, because a man should do the work in front of him. I just wouldn't do it first or with joy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between a drafter and an installer for the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The drafter makes a drawing, and it can be made by anyone or anything. The installer stands in the building and pulls the wire. A building has to be wired by hands, at least for now. So I'd like to have both, and be the one who understands the drawing and the wall.

say: We'll see who does the work **properly**, because someone has to answer for the building.
I'd rather see people **trained** than handed money.
think: Drawing layouts and sizing cables is the **thinking part**, so I'm exposed.
The firm may need fewer **drafters** and more installers and inspectors.
do: Spend more time on **site** and go for the installer certificate sooner.
Learn the layout software slowly as a **second opinion** if asked.
Keep my **savings** and ask my father about farm work if needed.
S1.quote: The drafter makes a drawing, and it can be made by anyone or anything. The installer stands in the building and pulls the wire.
fieldNote: Wants to be the one who understands **both** drawing and wall.
Learns software with **reluctance** but accepts it as duty.
Prefers training to handouts, in line with his views.

steps.text: Bring forward the installer certificate exam
Learn the layout software slowly and use it as a second check
Hold two months of costs untouched in savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and I'd say that governments and companies should have thought of this earlier. At the pub I'd say a man needs a trade and a family, and I'd hope the politicians don't just hand out money and call it a plan. I'd vote for anyone who put work first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. My job on the design side is thinking work, and if AI does it by 2028, my place at the firm is in question. I'd have about three more years before robots get to the hands-on part, which is a short window. My degree could be worth much less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my firm to move me to the installation team as quickly as possible, even at lower pay, so I'd be where hands are needed. I'd cut spending down to the basics and save as much as I can. I'd talk to my father about moving back to the farm for a time and doing some contract wiring locally. And I'd talk to Sofie about marrying earlier, because I'd want us to face it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I'd sleep badly, and I'd pray more. I'd feel like I've lost the plan I made at eighteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why marry earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a marriage is a promise to face hard times together, and hard times are coming. Sofie and I would also share one rent, which helps. It's the old way, but the old way works when money is short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who rushed this out because it makes them rich. I'm not against progress. But a man who builds a machine that takes thousands of jobs without asking should answer for it, and nobody does.

say: It's **too fast**, and governments should have thought of this earlier.
I'd vote for anyone who puts **work first**.
think: My design job is thinking work, so my place is **in question** in 2028.
I'd have only about **three years** before robots reach the hands-on part.
do: Ask to move to the **installation team**, even at lower pay.
Cut spending to **basics** and save hard.
feel: **Heavy**, with bad sleep and more prayer.
S2.quote: A marriage is a promise to face hard times together, and hard times are coming.
fieldNote: Fear turns to **family**: an earlier wedding as shared protection.
Blames the **people who rush** technology out for money.
Prayer and faith enter his answers for the first time.

steps.text: Ask to move onto the installation team at lower pay
Cut spending to rent, food and travel only
Plan an earlier wedding with Sofie to share one rent
Vote for the party that puts work and apprenticeships first

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough for sensible people to act. At the pub I'd say we need apprenticeships and trades back at the centre of things. To my boss I'd say that I'd like a path into the building side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel more settled than with two years. By 2031 I'd be 27, with five years of work behind me and probably a certified installer. I'd still worry about whether the design part of my job exists by then. I'd also worry about whether Sofie and I can afford a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work towards being a certified installer and a site supervisor, which is a job that needs a person walking around. I'd marry Sofie in about two years and start saving for a small house with a bit of land, which gives us a fall-back. I'd help my father with the farm, and ask if we could put solar panels on the barn, because I'd be the one who knows how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, I think. A bit anxious, but I'd know which way I was walking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why solar on the barn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's electrical work I understand, and it saves my father money. If I learn it on his barn, I can do it on others. A farm roof is a good place to learn, because nobody's in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still avoid AI tools in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, though less. I'd learn enough to know what they do, so I'm not the last to find out. I'd keep my own head for the numbers that matter.

say: Five years is long enough for **sensible people** to act.
We need **apprenticeships** and trades back at the centre.
think: By 2031 I'd have five years behind me and be a **certified installer**.
I still worry the **design** part of my job might not exist.
do: Become a certified installer and **site supervisor**.
Marry Sofie in two years and save for a small house with **land**.
Put **solar panels** on my father's barn.
feel: **Steady**, a bit anxious, but I'd know which way I was walking.
S3.quote: A farm roof is a good place to learn, because nobody's in a hurry.
fieldNote: Turns his **farm** background into a plan: solar on the barn.
Still keeps away from AI tools but allows **learning enough** not to be last.
Marriage and land as a fall-back are central.

steps.text: Qualify as a certified installer and then site supervisor
Marry Sofie in two years and save for a house with land
Fit solar panels on my father's barn
Learn what the AI design tools do, enough to judge them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, and we should use it to rebuild trades and local work. At the pub I'd say it will be fine if people stay steady. To Sofie I'd say we can plan our life as we'd always meant to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good, though not carefree. By 2036 I'd be 32, married with a child or two, and settled in a house. I'd have had time to become a good installer and maybe run a small team. I'd just worry that people would put it off, as people do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and marry within two years. We'd buy a small house with a workshop in about four years. I'd save and put a little into a farm-land share my father suggested. And I'd learn the new tools bit by bit, because after ten years they'd be part of every job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm. I'd be one of those people who goes to work and goes home and sleeps well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your views on AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If they're normal in ten years, I'd be foolish not to know them. I'd treat them like a power drill: I don't love it, but it's in the toolbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone puts the problem off, including me. My father says the barn roof gets fixed in summer, not in the storm. I'd write a plan in January and check it every year.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time**, so let's rebuild trades and local work.
It will be fine if people **stay steady**.
think: By 2036 I'd be 32, **married**, with a child or two, in a settled house.
I just worry people will **put it off**, as people do.
do: Keep the job and **marry** within two years.
Buy a small house with a **workshop** in about four years.
Learn the new tools **bit by bit**.
feel: **Quite calm**, the sort who goes to work and sleeps well.
S4.quote: My father says the barn roof gets fixed in summer, not in the storm.
fieldNote: His **resistance** to AI softens into treating it like a power drill.
Farm sayings anchor most of his best lines.

steps.text: Stay in the job and get promoted to senior designer
Marry Sofie and buy a small house with a workshop
Put a little into a farm-land share each month
Learn each new AI tool as it arrives at work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. The faster it comes, the less time a man has to find his feet. What would help is steady work, apprenticeships that lead to real jobs, and the family being close. I'd also want the companies behind it to answer for what it does to ordinary people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think I'm against the future because I like the old ways. I'm not. I just think a man should be able to answer for his own work, and that's a rule that doesn't age.

headlineQuote: A man should be able to answer for his own work, and that's a rule that doesn't age.
portrait: Felix Larsen is **22**, a junior electrical designer at a building services firm in Aarhus, from a dairy farm family.
He did electrical engineering, owes about **eleven thousand** and has two months of costs saved.
He's traditional, resistant to new technology and **never uses AI tools**; faith, family and work drive him.
Moods run from calm to **anxious** at AGI in two years, when he'd move to installation work and marry earlier.
He plans around the **trade**, a certificate, a house with land and solar on his father's barn.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because a man has **no time** to find his feet.
whatWouldHelp: Steady **work**, apprenticeships that lead to real jobs, family close by, and companies that answer for the harm.
